nameStory: Rosellinia takes its name from Italian botanist Salvatore Rosellini, who studied fungi in the 1800s. The species name 'subiculata' comes from the Latin word for 'underlayer,' referring to the yellowish mat of fungal threads that forms beneath the fruiting bodies like a tiny carpet.
description: Rosellinia subiculata is a small wood-decay fungus that creates tiny black bumps on rotting logs and branches. Each bump is actually a flask-shaped structure containing spores, and they're scattered randomly across the wood surface rather than clustered together. The fungus forms a distinctive yellowish mat of threads underneath these black fruiting bodies, making it easier to spot than many other wood fungi.

idTips.label: Yellow underlayer
idTips.description: Look for a bright yellow to golden mat of fuzzy fungal threads spreading beneath and around the black fruiting bodies - this feels slightly cottony when touched gently

idTips.label: Scattered black dots
idTips.description: Tiny black, hard bumps appear randomly scattered across the wood surface, each about the size of a pinhead and feeling firm like small pebbles

idTips.label: Single opening
idTips.description: Each black bump has just one tiny pore at the top (visible with a hand lens) rather than multiple openings

idTips.label: Decaying wood habitat
idTips.description: Found only on rotting hardwood logs and branches that feel soft and spongy, never on healthy or freshly fallen wood

idTips.label: No odor
idTips.description: Unlike many wood decay fungi, this species has no noticeable smell when you sniff close to the fruiting bodies

habitat: This fungus thrives on decaying hardwood logs and branches in moist New England forests, particularly in areas with good shade and humidity. You'll find it most commonly on fallen oak, maple, and birch wood in mixed deciduous and coniferous forests from sea level to mid-elevations. Look in areas where logs have been decomposing for at least a year or two.

seasonality.spring: Fresh fruiting bodies begin appearing as temperatures warm and moisture increases. The yellow underlayer is most vibrant and noticeable during wet spring conditions.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when both the black dots and yellow mat are most prominent and easy to spot. Dry periods may cause the yellow threads to fade temporarily.
seasonality.fall: Continues producing spores through autumn rains. The contrast between yellow threads and dark wood becomes especially striking as leaves fall and forest floors brighten.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting bodies persist but become less obvious. The yellow underlayer often fades or becomes hidden under snow and leaf litter.

funFact: This fungus is like a tiny biological recycling center - it can completely break down the tough lignin in wood (the same stuff that makes trees rigid) and transform a solid log into rich forest soil over several years, all while creating its own bright yellow 'welcome mat' to advertise its presence!
confusionNotes: Most other small black fungi on wood lack the distinctive yellow underlayer that makes Rosellinia subiculata unique. If you don't see yellow threads beneath the black dots, you're probably looking at a different species entirely. Memory trick: 'Rosellinia rolls out the yellow carpet.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being described as a plant pathogen that can affect citrus trees, in New England you'll only encounter this fungus as a harmless wood decomposer since citrus doesn't grow outdoors here. The same species can have different lifestyles in different climates and regions.
compareHints: Unlike its relative Rosellinia corticium, which forms more clustered fruiting bodies, R. subiculata creates scattered individual bumps across the wood surface. The yellow subiculum (underlayer) is also more prominent and widespread in R. subiculata, making it the more visually striking of the two species when you find them side by side on the same log.
